summary: The STIR certificate profile attests authority over telephone numbers to prevent number spoofing. This document details how that authority can be delegated from a parent certificate to a subordinate one. This supports cases such as a service provider giving credentials to an enterprise or other customer able to sign calls with STIR.

plainLanguage.summary: A phone company can give a business a permission slip to say that certain phone numbers really are the business's. This document explains how that permission slip is made to stop fake caller IDs.

questions: how to delegate authority over phone numbers
what is legitimate spoofing in stir
how does stir verify delegate certificates
subtitle: How a holder of phone-number authority can hand a slice of it to another party through a delegate certificate.

tldr.problem: STIR certificates prove who controls a telephone number, but callers whose outbound calls do not pass through the number's own service provider have no way to sign those calls, and signing with an unrelated credential looks like malicious spoofing.
tldr.mechanism: A parent certificate with a TNAuthList signs a delegate certificate whose TNAuthList is equal to or a subset of the parent's, and the PASSporT x5u link points to the whole certificate chain.
tldr.outcome: Enterprises and other customers can sign calls with their own delegated credentials, and verification services validate the full chain back to a trust anchor.

facts.label: Delegate scope rule
facts.value: Equal to or a subset of the parent's TNAuthList

today: RFC 9060 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2021, and the unit metadata lists nothing that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself says that STIR was only starting to see deployment when it was written, and that a TLS-subcerts-style alternative would be built only if the market requires it.

sections.title: Why Delegation Is Needed
sections.content:
STIR (Secure Telephone Identity Revisited) uses certificates to show who controls a telephone number, as described in RFC 8226. Those credentials let authentication services sign PASSporT objects carried in SIP requests. The most pressing need for delegation arises when callers want to use a particular calling number but their outbound calls will not pass through the authentication service of the provider that controls that number.

The RFC gives two examples. An enterprise may route calls through several service providers by least-cost routing, even though only one assigned it the number. A user may also roam to a different network and still want to show the main callback number for their business, which the RFC calls legitimate spoofing.

Without delegation, outbound carriers may have to sign calls with credentials that do not cover the originating number. That is hard to tell apart from malicious spoofing, and if it becomes widespread it could erode trust in STIR overall.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine you borrow your friend's phone to call home but want it to show your own number. A signed note from the number's owner proves it is allowed.

sections.title: Delegate Certificates and Encompassing
sections.content:
A STIR delegate certificate is a certificate containing a TNAuthList object that has been signed with the private key of a parent certificate that itself contains a TNAuthList (by value or by reference). The parent needs a basic constraints extension with the cA boolean set to true, and every delegate identifies its parent with an Authority Key Identifier extension.

Each delegate's TNAuthList MUST be equal to or a subset of its parent's scope, a rule the RFC calls being encompassed. For example, a parent with authority over +1-212-555-1000 through 1999 could give one delegate the range +1-212-555-1500 through 1599 and another the single number +1-212-555-1824.

Delegates MAY also have cA set to true so they can delegate further. Only end-entity certificates can sign PASSporTs, so such a holder creates a separate end-entity certificate with the same or a smaller scope for signing.
sections.plainLanguage: A parent can only hand out part of what it owns, like giving a child some of its pocket money but never more than it has.

sections.title: Scope of Delegation
sections.content:
A TNAuthList may hold Service Provider Codes (SPCs), telephone number ranges, or a mix. An SPC-only parent may explicitly delegate individual numbers or ranges to a child. Permissions are additive, so a certificate's scope is the superset of everything listed, even if some of it is redundant.

For entities with large or fast-changing allocations, a certificate can carry the TNAuthList by reference, with a URL pointing to a secure, dynamically updated list, as described in Section 10.1 of RFC 8226. Entities with simple, long-lived assignments, such as a block of a thousand numbers or a freephone number tied to a brand, can just list ranges by value. Path construction treats by-reference lists as if they were included by value.

The RFC notes a trade-off over when to check encompassing: at issuance, at call verification, or both. It is generally desirable to offload as much as possible to the certification process, because verification happens during call setup and extra network lookups could add perceptible delay.
sections.plainLanguage: The permission slip can list numbers directly, or point to a list that is kept up to date somewhere else.

sections.title: Signing and Verifying with Delegates
sections.content:
Authentication services SHOULD NOT use a delegate certificate without validating that its scope is encompassed by its parent's, and if that parent has its own parent, the whole certification path SHOULD be validated. The entity does not have to be its own authentication service: any service holding the delegate's private key can sign, including one run by an outbound provider, a third party, or the SIP user agent itself.

When signing, the authentication service MUST provide an x5u link that covers the entire certification path, not only the delegate certificate. The verification service dereferences x5u, receives a certificate list, and MUST validate every credential in it, finding each parent through its Authority Key Identifier.

STIR assumes a rigid hierarchical model rather than letting relying parties build their own paths. If the certificates do not lead to a trust anchor the verifier trusts, it treats this like any untrusted root, and in SIP it MAY return a 437 Unsupported Credential response.
sections.plainLanguage: The person checking the note follows the chain of signatures back to someone they already trust. If the chain breaks, they do not believe the note.

sections.title: Delivering the Certificate Chain
sections.content:
The PASSporT x5u element conveys a URL, commonly HTTPS, where verifiers get the signing certificate. For delegates it points to a certificate list. The baseline JWS format also has an x5c element for chains, but because paths are already delivered through x5u in practice, the RFC RECOMMENDS continuing to use x5u, and x5c is OPTIONAL where known to be supported.

The list is a concatenation of PEM certificates of type application/pem-certificate-chain, defined in RFC 8555. It MUST be ordered from the signer to the trust anchor: the signing certificate, then its parent, then grandparents and so on. The key identifier in the Authority Key Identifier extension of each certificate MUST appear in the Subject Key Identifier extension of the next one, all the way down the chain.
sections.plainLanguage: The signed note comes with a stack of papers, ordered from the one who signed it up to the most trusted person.

sections.title: CAs, ACME and Multiple Certificates
sections.content:
A service provider holding a CA certificate may delegate from it as it sees fit, but that does not make it a certification authority itself, which is a job requiring specialized expertise such as maintaining revocation lists and publishing practice statements. A third-party CA can issue the delegate certificates, with the provider acting as a Token Authority. All CAs must detail in their policies a requirement to validate that a delegate is encompassed by its parent, possibly using industry databases or an Authority Token.

The RFC anticipates that delegate certificates will be acquired through ACME (RFC 8555). An entity requests an Authority Token from the parent with the desired TNAuthList, then presents it to a CA. If the entity plans further subdelegation, it should request a token with the ca flag set. Providers wanting to age out delegated certificates quickly can use ACME STAR (RFC 8739).

An enterprise with numbers from several carriers may end up holding a keyring of certificates. Possible fixes include cross-certification through the Authority Information Access field or a bridge CA, but these would complicate path reconstruction and need further specification.
sections.plainLanguage: A phone company does not have to become a certificate office itself. It can ask an existing office to print the notes for its customers.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC is entirely about security. It hopes that delegation will improve the STIR ecosystem by replacing unauthenticated legitimate spoofing with signing. Much of the security depends on the encompassing semantics. Delegating from an SPC-based list to number ranges may need industry databases that track a provider's numbers, and in some environments such databases might not exist, so how encompassing is policed is outside this document.

By-reference TNAuthLists can change over time, so a relying party might accept a number at one point and reject it later. If the HTTPS service holding the list is poorly secured, that is a vulnerability too. The CA that issued the delegate populates the URL in the AIA field and is responsible for a secure choice.

On privacy, a certificate with a narrow number range potentially reveals information about the entities placing calls. Because the range is a necessary superset of the openly signaled calling number, the risks are not substantially greater than baseline STIR.
sections.plainLanguage: The list of allowed numbers must be guarded well, because anyone who can change it can change who is trusted.

viz.caption: CHAIN ORDER IN THE X5U CERTIFICATE LIST

layers.label: Signing certificate
layers.detail: Used to sign the PASSporT; listed first

layers.label: Parent certificate
layers.detail: Its Subject Key Identifier matches the first certificate's Authority Key Identifier

layers.label: Grandparents and so on
layers.detail: Continue in order up the path
